hmmt-feb-2011-algcalc-01.title: Discriminants cannot all be nonnegative
hmmt-feb-2011-algcalc-01.body:
If all three quadratics had real roots, their discriminants would be nonnegative:
$$b^2\ge 4ac,\qquad c^2\ge 4ab,\qquad a^2\ge 4bc.$$
All sides are positive, so multiplying gives $(abc)^2\ge 64(abc)^2$, impossible because $abc>0$. So at least one quadratic has no real roots, and the total is at most $2+2=4$.

**Example with 4 roots.** Take $(a,b,c)=(1,5,6)$. Then $x^2+5x+6$ has roots $-2,-3$; $5x^2+6x+1$ has roots $-1,-\tfrac15$; and $6x^2+x+5$ has discriminant $1-120<0$, so no real roots. That is $4$ real roots.

**Answer: 4**

hmmt-feb-2011-algcalc-02.title: He must pass through the middle of every row
hmmt-feb-2011-algcalc-02.body:
Call a move $R$ (one square right) or $U$ (one square left and one up).

- In column 1 the only legal move is $R$ (a left move is impossible), so Josh is forced into column 2.
- In column 3 the only legal move is $U$ (he cannot move right), which lands in column 2 of the next row.
- Whenever he enters a new row he arrives in column 1 (from column 2 by $U$) or column 2 (from column 3 by $U$). If in column 1, the next move is forced to $R$, bringing him to column 2.

So he stands on the center square of every row. From the center square of row $k$ there are exactly two ways to reach the center square of row $k+1$:
1. $R$ to column 3, then $U$ to column 2 of row $k+1$;
2. $U$ to column 1 of row $k+1$, then $R$ to column 2.

He reaches the center of row 1 in exactly one way (a single $R$ from the start). Hence the number of ways to reach the center of row $n$ is $2^{n-1}$.

**Answer: $2^{n-1}$**

hmmt-feb-2011-algcalc-03.title: Trap the graph in a parallelogram
hmmt-feb-2011-algcalc-03.body:
By the Mean Value Theorem $|f(x)|\le 2x$ and $|1-f(x)|\le 2(1-x)$, so the graph of $f$ lies between the lines of slope $\pm2$ through $(0,0)$ and through $(1,1)$. These four lines bound the parallelogram with vertices $(0,0)$, $(0.75,1.5)$, $(1,1)$, $(0.25,-0.5)$.

The graph cannot leave the parallelogram, and smoothing the corners one can find admissible functions whose graphs come arbitrarily close to its upper boundary and arbitrarily close to its lower boundary. Therefore the integral takes every value strictly between the area under the lower boundary and the area under the upper boundary (and no others), so $b-a$ is the area of the parallelogram.

For $0\le x\le\tfrac14$ the vertical thickness is $2x-(-2x)=4x$, for $\tfrac14\le x\le\tfrac34$ it is $2x-(2x-1)=1$, and for $\tfrac34\le x\le1$ it is $(3-2x)-(2x-1)=4-4x$. Hence
$$b-a=\int_0^{1/4}4x\,dx+\int_{1/4}^{3/4}1\,dx+\int_{3/4}^{1}(4-4x)\,dx=\tfrac18+\tfrac12+\tfrac18=\tfrac34.$$

**Answer: $\tfrac34$**

hmmt-feb-2011-algcalc-04.title: Reduce to a ratio of areas
hmmt-feb-2011-algcalc-04.body:
Since $E$ is on $AC$ and $F$ on $BC$, the line $EF\parallel AD$ cuts off a piece next to vertex $C$. The three parts have equal area exactly when triangle $ADB$ is one third of the whole and triangle $ADC$ is cut by $EF$ into two equal halves. Such $E,F$ exist (a parallel to $AD$ can cut off any prescribed fraction of triangle $ADC$) if and only if
$$[ADC]=2[ADB].$$
The two triangles share the altitude from $A$, so $\dfrac{[ADC]}{[ADB]}=\dfrac{DC}{DB}=\dfrac{AC}{AB}$ by the angle bisector theorem. The condition becomes $AC=2AB=14$.

With $AB=7$, $AC=14$, the side $BC=d$ must satisfy the triangle inequality: $d+7>14$ and $d<21$, so $7<d<21$. The integers $8,9,\dots,20$ give $13$ values.

**Answer: 13**

hmmt-feb-2011-algcalc-05.title: Symmetric system of equations mod 7
hmmt-feb-2011-algcalc-05.body:
For $1\le k\le6$ let $x_k$ be the probability that the player about to roll wins when the tally is $\equiv k\pmod 7$. After the roll the tally is $\equiv l$ for each residue $l\ne k$ with probability $\tfrac16$ each. If $l\equiv0$ the roller wins at once; otherwise the opponent is to roll at residue $l$ and the roller wins with probability $1-x_l$. So
$$x_k=\frac16+\frac16\sum_{\substack{1\le l\le6\\ l\ne k}}(1-x_l)=\frac16+\frac{5-s+x_k}{6},\qquad s=\sum_{l=1}^6x_l .$$
This gives $5x_k=6-s$ for every $k$, so all $x_k$ are equal to some $x$ with $s=6x$: $5x=6-6x$, $x=\tfrac6{11}$.

Nathaniel cannot win on his first roll (the tally is at most $6$), so after it Obediah faces a nonzero residue and wins with probability $\tfrac6{11}$. Hence Nathaniel wins with probability $1-\tfrac6{11}=\tfrac5{11}$ (the game ends with probability $1$).

**Answer: $\tfrac5{11}$**

hmmt-feb-2011-algcalc-06.title: Shift by one
hmmt-feb-2011-algcalc-06.body:
Notice $a\star b+1=ab+a+b+1=(a+1)(b+1)$. Define $\varphi(a)=a+1$; then $\varphi(a\star b)=\varphi(a)\varphi(b)$, so $\star$ corresponds to ordinary multiplication after adding $1$ (in particular $\star$ is commutative and associative).

Therefore
$$1\star(2\star(\cdots(99\star100)))+1=(1+1)(2+1)(3+1)\cdots(100+1)=2\cdot3\cdots101=101!.$$
The value is $101!-1$.

**Answer: $101!-1$**

hmmt-feb-2011-algcalc-06.title: Induction
hmmt-feb-2011-algcalc-06.body:
$\star$ is commutative, and associative since $a\star(b\star c)=abc+ab+ac+bc+a+b+c=(a\star b)\star c$. So the expression equals $(\cdots((1\star2)\star3)\cdots)\star100$. By induction this left-nested product up to $n$ equals $(n+1)!-1$: the case $n=2$ is $1\star2=5=3!-1$, and $((n+1)!-1)\star(n+1)=(n+1)!(n+1)-(n+1)+(n+1)!-1+(n+1)=(n+2)!-1$. For $n=100$ we get $101!-1$.

**Answer: $101!-1$**

hmmt-feb-2011-algcalc-07.title: Squeeze the difference quotient
hmmt-feb-2011-algcalc-07.body:
We have $\tfrac13=.333\ldots$. The function $f$ is increasing: if $x<y$ and their expansions first differ at digit $k$, then $a_k<a_k'$, and the tails of $f$ differ by less than $9\sum_{m>k}10^{-2m}<10^{-2k}$, so $f(x)<f(y)$.

Changing the $n$-th digit of $\tfrac13$ from $3$ to $4$ or to $2$ gives $\tfrac13\pm10^{-n}$ and
$$f\!\left(\tfrac13\pm10^{-n}\right)-f\!\left(\tfrac13\right)=\pm10^{-2n}.$$
Take $h$ with $10^{-n-1}\le|h|<10^{-n}$. Since $f$ is increasing, $\tfrac13+h$ lies between $\tfrac13-10^{-n}$ and $\tfrac13+10^{-n}$, so $\left|f\!\left(\tfrac13+h\right)-f\!\left(\tfrac13\right)\right|\le10^{-2n}$, and
$$\left|\frac{f(\tfrac13+h)-f(\tfrac13)}{h}\right|\le\frac{10^{-2n}}{10^{-n-1}}=10^{1-n}.$$
As $h\to0$ we have $n\to\infty$, so the quotient tends to $0$. Hence $f'(\tfrac13)=0$.

**Answer: 0**

hmmt-feb-2011-algcalc-08.title: Factor and compare the factors
hmmt-feb-2011-algcalc-08.body:
Write $2x^2+x-6=(2x-3)(x+2)=p^k$ with $p$ prime, $k\ge1$. Put $u=2x-3$, $v=x+2$; then $2v-u=7$ and $uv=p^k>0$, so $u,v$ have the same sign and each is $\pm$ a power of $p$ (possibly $\pm1$).

**Case 1: one of $u,v$ is $\pm1$.**
- $u=1$: $x=2$, product $4=2^2$. ✓
- $u=-1$: $x=1$, product $-3<0$. ✗
- $v=1$: $x=-1$, product $-5<0$. ✗
- $v=-1$: $x=-3$, product $9=3^2$. ✓

**Case 2: $|u|,|v|\ge p$ both.** Then $p\mid u$ and $p\mid v$, so $p\mid 2v-u=7$ and $p=7$: $u=\pm7^a$, $v=\pm7^b$ with $a,b\ge1$.
- Positive signs: $2\cdot7^b-7^a=7$, i.e. $2\cdot7^{b-1}-7^{a-1}=1$. If $b=1$ then $a=1$. If $b\ge2$, then $7^{a-1}\equiv-1\pmod 7$, impossible. So $u=v=7$, $x=5$, product $49$. ✓
- Negative signs: $7^{a-1}-2\cdot7^{b-1}=1$. If $b=1$: $7^{a-1}=3$, impossible. If $b\ge2$: $7^{a-1}\equiv1\pmod7$ forces $a=1$, giving $2\cdot7^{b-1}=0$, impossible.

So the solutions are $x=-3,2,5$ (check: $2\cdot25+5-6=49$).

**Answer: $x=-3,\,2,\,5$**

hmmt-feb-2011-algcalc-09.title: Inclusion-exclusion
hmmt-feb-2011-algcalc-09.body:
Quadrilaterals $ACDM$ and $BFEM$ overlap exactly in $MXZY$, and the part of the hexagon covered by neither is the union of the three triangles $BXC$, $AYF$, $ABZ$. Hence
$$[ABCDEF]=[ACDM]+[BFEM]-[MXZY]+[BXC]+[AYF]+[ABZ],$$
so the required quantity equals $[ABCDEF]-[ACDM]-[BFEM]$.

Let $O$ be the center. $[ADM]=\tfrac12[ADE]=[ODE]$ (as $O$ is the midpoint of $AD$), and $[ODE]=[ABC]$ because $\sin60^\circ=\sin120^\circ$ and the triangles have two sides equal to the hexagon's side. Thus
$$[ACDM]=[ACD]+[ADM]=[ACD]+[ABC]=[ABCD]=\tfrac12[ABCDEF],$$
since diagonal $AD$ halves the hexagon. By symmetry $[BFEM]=\tfrac12$ as well. The value is $1-\tfrac12-\tfrac12=0$.

**Answer: 0**

hmmt-feb-2011-algcalc-10.title: f applied three times is the identity
hmmt-feb-2011-algcalc-10.body:
Let $y=x^{2011}$. Then $f(x)^{2011}=\dfrac1{1-y}$, so on $2011$-th powers $f$ acts as $y\mapsto\dfrac1{1-y}$. Applying it again: $\dfrac{1}{1-\frac1{1-y}}=\dfrac{y-1}{y}$, and once more: $\dfrac{1}{1-\frac{y-1}{y}}=y$. Thus $f(f(f(x)))=x$ (2011 is odd, so real roots are unambiguous).

Since $2010=3\cdot670$, applying $f$ $2010$ times returns the starting value $2011$, and raising it to the $2011$th power gives $2011^{2011}$.

**Answer: $2011^{2011}$**

hmmt-feb-2011-algcalc-11.title: Substitute x = e^u and use the Gamma integral
Integration by parts
hmmt-feb-2011-algcalc-11.body:
Let $I_n=\int_1^\infty\frac{(\ln x)^n}{x^{2011}}dx$. Integrating by parts with $u=(\ln x)^n$, $dv=x^{-2011}dx$ (the boundary terms vanish since $\ln1=0$ and $(\ln x)^n/x^{2010}\to0$) gives $I_n=\dfrac{n}{2010}I_{n-1}$. With $I_0=\int_1^\infty x^{-2011}dx=\dfrac1{2010}$ we get $I_n=\dfrac{n!}{2010^{n+1}}$, so $I_{2011}=\dfrac{2011!}{2010^{2012}}$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{2011!}{2010^{2012}}$**

hmmt-feb-2011-algcalc-12.title: One of the two inner equations must have a double root
hmmt-feb-2011-algcalc-12.body:
If $f$ had at most one real root $r$, then the roots of $f(f(x))$ solve $f(x)=r$, at most $2$ of them. So $f$ has two distinct roots $r_1\ne r_2$, and the roots of $f(f(x))$ are the solutions of $f(x)=r_1$ and of $f(x)=r_2$ (disjoint sets). To have exactly three, one of these equations has exactly one root, say $f(x)=r_1$, i.e. $x^2+6x+c-r_1=0$ has a double root: $c-r_1=9$. Then $r_1=c-9$ is a root of $f$:
$$(c-9)^2+6(c-9)+c=0\iff c^2-11c+27=0\iff c=\frac{11\pm\sqrt{13}}2.$$
Now check each value.
- $c=\frac{11-\sqrt{13}}2$: the roots of $f$ are $-\frac{7+\sqrt{13}}2$ and $-\frac{5-\sqrt{13}}2$. The equation $f(x)=-\frac{7+\sqrt{13}}2=c-9$ has the double root $x=-3$. The other value $-\frac{5-\sqrt{13}}{2}$ exceeds the minimum value $f(-3)=c-9$, so $f(x)=$ it has two distinct real solutions. Total: $3$ distinct roots. ✓
- $c=\frac{11+\sqrt{13}}2$: $f(-3)=c-9=-\frac{7-\sqrt{13}}2$ is the minimum of $f$ and a root of $f$; the other root of $f$ is $-\frac{5+\sqrt{13}}{2}$, which is below the minimum, so $f(x)=$ it has no real solution. Then $f(f(x))$ has only the root $-3$. ✗

**Answer: $c=\dfrac{11-\sqrt{13}}{2}$**

hmmt-feb-2011-algcalc-13.title: Self-consistency by scaling
hmmt-feb-2011-algcalc-13.body:
Let $f(r)$ be the expected red area (for the player who throws first) on a board of radius $r$. By scaling, $f(r)=\pi x\,r^2$ for a constant $x$; we want $f(1)=\pi x$.

Suppose the first dart lands at distance $\rho$ from the center of the unit board. Then $O_1$ has radius $1-\rho$. The first player colors the ring of area $\pi-\pi(1-\rho)^2$. Now the opponent throws first on $O_1$, whose total area is $\pi(1-\rho)^2$; the opponent's expected area there is $f(1-\rho)$, so the first player expects $\pi(1-\rho)^2-f(1-\rho)$ more. In total $\pi-f(1-\rho)$.

The dart is uniform on the disk, so $\rho$ has density $2\rho\,d\rho$ on $[0,1]$:
$$\pi x=\int_0^1\bigl(\pi-\pi x(1-\rho)^2\bigr)2\rho\,d\rho=\pi-2\pi x\int_0^1\rho(1-\rho)^2d\rho=\pi-2\pi x\cdot\frac1{12}.$$
So $\pi x\left(1+\tfrac16\right)=\pi$, giving $x=\tfrac67$ and $f(1)=\tfrac{6\pi}7$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{6\pi}{7}$**

hmmt-feb-2011-algcalc-14.title: Falling-factorial basis
hmmt-feb-2011-algcalc-14.body:
Let $x^{\underline i}=x(x-1)\cdots(x-i+1)$ (with $x^{\underline0}=1$). Every integer polynomial of degree at most $5$ can be written uniquely as $P(x)=\sum_{i=0}^5a_ix^{\underline i}$ with integer $a_i$ (induct on the degree: subtract the leading term and use that $x^{\underline i}$ is monic of degree $i$).

Then $P(i)=a_i\,i!+a_{i-1}\,i^{\underline{i-1}}+\dots+a_0$, which depends only on $a_0,\dots,a_i$.
- $a_0=P(0)$ can be any of the $120$ integers in $[0,120)$.
- Once $a_0,\dots,a_{i-1}$ are fixed, $P(i)\equiv a_{i-1}i^{\underline{i-1}}+\dots+a_0\pmod{i!}$ is determined mod $i!$ and changing $a_i$ shifts $P(i)$ by multiples of $i!$, so $P(i)$ can be any number in $[0,120)$ with the right residue: exactly $\dfrac{120}{i!}$ choices (note $i!\mid120$ for $i\le5$). Choosing $a_i$ does not change $P(0),\dots,P(i-1)$.

The total is
$$\prod_{i=0}^5\frac{120}{i!}=120\cdot120\cdot60\cdot20\cdot5\cdot1=86\,400\,000.$$

**Answer: 86400000**

hmmt-feb-2011-algcalc-15.title: Bounds
hmmt-feb-2011-algcalc-15.body:
Since $f\le1$, the integral is at most $1$, attained by $f\equiv1$.

The condition says $f=1$ at every point of the range of $f$. Since $1$ is in the range, $f(1)=1$. Let $c=\min f$ (attained by continuity); $c$ is in the range, so $f(c)=1$. If $c=1$ then $f\equiv1$. Otherwise $c<1$: by the Intermediate Value Theorem $f$ takes every value in $[c,1]$, so $f(x)=1$ for all $x\in[c,1]$. Hence
$$\int_0^1f=\int_0^cf+(1-c)>c\cdot c+(1-c)=\left(c-\tfrac12\right)^2+\tfrac34\ge\tfrac34 .$$
The inequality $\int_0^cf>c^2$ is strict because $f\ge c$ with $f(c)=1>c$ and $f$ continuous. So the integral lies in $(\tfrac34,1]$.

**Every value occurs.** For $0<c<1$ and $0<\varepsilon\le c$ let $f=c$ on $[0,c-\varepsilon]$, linear from $c$ up to $1$ on $[c-\varepsilon,c]$, and $f=1$ on $[c,1]$. Then $f(f(x))=1$ and $\int_0^1f=c^2+1-c+\tfrac{(1-c)\varepsilon}{2}$, which varies continuously over the interval $\bigl(c^2-c+1,\ c^2-c+1+\tfrac{c(1-c)}2\bigr]$ as $\varepsilon$ varies. As $c$ runs through $(0,\tfrac12]$ these intervals have lower endpoints decreasing continuously from $1$ to $\tfrac34$ and cover all of $(\tfrac34,1)$; $f\equiv1$ gives $1$.

**Answer: the interval $\left(\tfrac34,1\right]$**

hmmt-feb-2011-algcalc-16.title: Lower bound |r_2| > 2
hmmt-feb-2011-algcalc-16.body:
Here $g_1=r_3>g_0=0$. Consider $f(x)-x$. By (i), $f(g_{2i+1})=g_{2i+2}<g_{2i+1}$, so $f(x)-x<0$ somewhere; as it is an upward parabola it has two real roots $a<b$, and $f(x)-x=(x-a)(x-b)$. Comparing coefficients, $a+b=r_2+1$.

The equation $f(x)=b$ has the roots $b$ and $c=r_2-b=a-1$, and $f(x)>b$ exactly when $x<c$ or $x>b$. By (ii) and (iii) some term exceeds $b$; let $g_j$ be the first. Then $g_{j-1}\le b$ and $f(g_{j-1})>b$, so $g_{j-1}<c=a-1$. Since $g_{j-1}=f(g_{j-2})\ge\min f$, the minimum of $f$ is below $a-1$. The vertex is at $v=\frac{a+b-1}2$ and, with $d=b-a$,
$$f(v)=(v-a)(v-b)+v=-\frac{d^2-1}{4}+\frac{a+b-1}2<a-1 .$$
Multiplying by $4$ and simplifying gives $d^2-2d-3>0$, i.e. $d>3$.

The discriminant of $f(x)-x$ is $d^2=(r_2+1)^2-4r_3$, so $(r_2+1)^2=d^2+4r_3>9$. Hence $r_2>2$ or $r_2<-4$; in both cases $|r_2|>2$.

**Sharpness.** We show $|r_2|$ can be made arbitrarily close to $2$. For $\varepsilon>0$ let $h(x)=x^2-2-\varepsilon$ and fix $N\ge2012$. Put $G_{2N+1}=2+\varepsilon$, $G_{i}=-\sqrt{G_{i+1}+2+\varepsilon}$ for $i=2N,2N-1,\dots,0$ (then $h(G_i)=G_{i+1}$), and $G_{i+1}=h(G_i)$ for $i>2N$. Let $l<0$ be the negative fixed point of $h$. Backward induction shows $G_{2i}<l<G_{2i+1}$ for $0\le i\le N-1$, which gives the oscillation (i). For $i\ge2N+1$ the sequence is increasing because $h(x)-x=x(x-1)-2-\varepsilon>0$ for $x\ge2+\varepsilon$ and it grows faster and faster, giving (ii) and (iii). Now set $f(x)=h(x+G_0)-G_0=x^2+2G_0x+\text{const}$; then $g_i=G_i-G_0$, so $f$ has the same properties, with $r_2=-2G_0$. As $N\to\infty$ and $\varepsilon\to0$, $G_0\to-1$: the map $x\mapsto-\sqrt{x+2}$ sends $-2\cos\theta$ to $-2\cos\frac{\pi-\theta}2$, so repeated application from $2=-2\cos\pi$ converges to $-2\cos\frac\pi3=-1$ (and the dependence on $\varepsilon$ is continuous). Thus $|r_2|=2|G_0|\to2$.

Thus the greatest such $A$ is $2$.

**Answer: 2**

hmmt-feb-2011-algcalc-17.title: f' never vanishes, so f is monotone
hmmt-feb-2011-algcalc-17.body:
Suppose $f'(y)=0$ for some $y$. By continuity of $f'$ there is an interval $(c,d)\ni y$ on which $|f'|\le\tfrac12$. Pick $n$ so large that $(c,d)$ contains two consecutive points $\frac k{2^n},\frac{k+1}{2^n}$; one of $k,k+1$ is odd (call it $a$) and the other is even, $a'=2^m a''$ with $m\ge1$, $a''$ odd. By hypothesis $f(\frac a{2^n})=\frac b{2^n}$ with $b$ odd, and, applying the hypothesis at level $n-m$ to $\frac{a'}{2^n}=\frac{a''}{2^{n-m}}$, $f(\frac{a'}{2^n})=\frac{b''}{2^{n-m}}=\frac{2^mb''}{2^n}$ with $b''$ odd, so $2^nf(\frac{a'}{2^n})$ is even. Therefore $2^nf$ takes an odd value at one of the two points and an even value at the other, and the two values differ by an odd integer. The difference quotient of $f$ between the two points is $\frac{f(\frac{k+1}{2^n})-f(\frac k{2^n})}{2^{-n}}=2^nf(\tfrac{k+1}{2^n})-2^nf(\tfrac k{2^n})$, an odd integer, so its absolute value is at least $1$. By the Mean Value Theorem $f'$ takes this value somewhere in $(c,d)$, contradicting $|f'|\le\tfrac12$ there. So $f'$ never vanishes; being continuous it has constant sign, and $f$ is strictly monotone.

**Increasing case.** For $n=1,a=1$ we get $f(\tfrac12)=\tfrac12$. Inductively, if $f$ fixes every dyadic rational with denominator $2^{m}$, $m\le n$, then for odd $a<2^{n+1}$, $f(\frac a{2^{n+1}})=\frac b{2^{n+1}}$ with $b$ odd lies strictly between $f(\frac{a-1}{2^{n+1}})=\frac{a-1}{2^{n+1}}$ and $f(\frac{a+1}{2^{n+1}})=\frac{a+1}{2^{n+1}}$, forcing $b=a$. Dyadic rationals are dense and $f$ is continuous, so $f(x)=x$ and $f'(\frac12)=1$.

**Decreasing case.** The function $g(x)=1-f(x)$ also satisfies the hypothesis (if $f(\frac a{2^n})=\frac b{2^n}$ with $b$ odd, then $g(\frac a{2^n})=\frac{2^n-b}{2^n}$ with $2^n-b$ odd), maps $(0,1)$ to $(0,1)$ and is increasing, so by the previous case $g(x)=x$, i.e. $f(x)=1-x$ and $f'(\frac12)=-1$. Both functions satisfy the hypothesis (for odd $a$, $2^n-a$ is odd). Hence the set of possible values is $\{-1,1\}$.

**Answer: $\{-1,\ 1\}$**

hmmt-feb-2011-algcalc-19.title: Dominant singularity at x = 1
hmmt-feb-2011-algcalc-19.body:
For $|x|\le1$, $|x+x^5|\le2$ with equality only when $x=x^5=1$. So $x=1$ is the only root of $2-x-x^5$ in the closed unit disk, and it is simple: $\frac{d}{dx}(2-x-x^5)=-6$ at $x=1$. All other roots lie strictly outside the unit circle.

Hence $\dfrac1{2-x-x^5}=\dfrac{1/6}{1-x}+h(x)$ with $h$ analytic in a disk $|x|<R$, $R>1$ (the residue at $x=1$ is $\lim_{x\to1}\frac{1-x}{2-x-x^5}=\frac16$). Raise to the $2011$th power and expand binomially:
$$F(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{2011}\binom{2011}{k}\frac{(1/6)^k}{(1-x)^k}h(x)^{2011-k}.$$
The coefficient of $x^n$ in $(1-x)^{-k}$ is $\binom{n+k-1}{k-1}\sim\frac{n^{k-1}}{(k-1)!}$, and multiplying by an analytic factor in $|x|<R$ changes only lower-order terms (and the coefficient of the leading term by a factor equal to its value at $x=1$). So the largest growth comes from $k=2011$, where $h^{0}=1$:
$$a_n\sim\left(\tfrac16\right)^{2011}\binom{n+2010}{2010}\sim\frac{1}{6^{2011}\,2010!}\,n^{2010}.$$
Hence $d=2010$ and $c=\dfrac{1}{6^{2011}\cdot2010!}$.

**Answer: $(c,d)=\left(\dfrac1{6^{2011}\,2010!},\,2010\right)$**

hmmt-feb-2011-algcalc-20.title: Complex numbers
hmmt-feb-2011-algcalc-20.body:
Let $z_n=a_n+b_ni$ and $s_n=\sqrt{1+a_n^2+b_n^2}$. The recursion says $z_{n+1}=z_n(s_n+i)$. Then $|z_{n+1}|^2=|z_n|^2(s_n^2+1)=|z_n|^2(|z_n|^2+2)$, so $1+|z_{n+1}|^2=(1+|z_n|^2)^2$, and $s_{n+1}=s_n^2$. Since $s_0=\sqrt9=3$, we get $s_n=3^{2^n}$ and
$$z_4=(2+2i)(3+i)(3^2+i)(3^4+i)(3^8+i).$$
Expanding $\prod_{j=0}^3(3^{2^j}+i)$ over subsets of factors, each exponent $m=\sum_{j\in S}2^j$ ($0\le m\le15$) appears once, with coefficient $i^{4-s(m)}$ where $s(m)$ is the number of $1$s in the binary expansion of $m$:
$$x+yi=\sum_{m=0}^{15}i^{4-s(m)}3^m .$$
So the digit of $3^m$ in $x$ is $+1$ if $s(m)\equiv0$, $-1$ if $s(m)\equiv2\pmod 4$, $0$ if $s(m)$ is odd; in $y$ it is $-1$ if $s(m)\equiv1$, $+1$ if $s(m)\equiv3\pmod4$, $0$ if $s(m)$ is even (balanced ternary digits). Converting, $x=221211221122001_3$ and $y=110022202212120_3$ in ordinary ternary (that is, $x$ and $y$ in base 3). Finally $a_4+b_4i=(2+2i)(x+yi)$ gives $a_4=2x-2y$, $b_4=2x+2y$.

In decimal $a_4=14\,375\,528$ and $b_4=40\,575\,416$, and in base $3$:
$$a_4=1000001100111222_3,\qquad b_4=2211100110000012_3.$$

**Answer: $a_4=1000001100111222_3$, $b_4=2211100110000012_3$**
